messages.subject: CODEX
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Good morning or afternoon.

I am currently enrolled in the master's program of biostatistics and I hope to start my thesis on the application of CODEX in finding the CNVs among n samples (n>30). Now my question is:

1. What are the minimum requirements for a computer in order to run your package? We are going to find CNVs in the whole exome sequencing of at least 30 people.

2. If I have understand it well, the chromosome formats should be consistent between the .bed and the .bam files. Now I need to know that we should have 23 bam files of chromosomes for each person and 23 bed files for each chromosome seperately? or a bam file consisting of 23 chromosomes for each person and a bed file for all the chromosomes are required?

thanks in advance

messages.subject: Re: CODEX
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX!

CODEX is a R-package. You can download it directly from Bioconductor under windows, mac, or linux. You can directly run CODEX on your laptop however you have to store your bam files locally. To run CODEX on one chromosome, it will take around 2 hours on your computer. If you want to run your jobs (for example, separated by chr) in parallel, it’s better if you run it on a cluster.

You can use the original mapped and sorted bam files (together with .bai files) and a single bed file. The bam file for each sample has reads specifying which chromosome it gets mapped to; the bed file (exonic target for all samples) has each line specifying the chromosome, start base pair, and ending base pair. You don’t need to separate input by chromosome. CODEX normalizes and segments each chromosome separately and the chromosome format should be concordant with what is given in bam and in bed.

Let me know if you have further questions,
Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: question on CODEX: tuning of optimal K?
messages.subject_clean: question on CODEX: tuning of optimal K?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mari,

If the BIC (default by CODEX) chooses the optimal K at 2 I think you should keep it as it is. You can use Z = log(Y_qc/pmax(Yhat[[optK]],0.001)) to get the normalized Z score. Each row corresponds to an exon and each column corresponds to a sample. You know which sample (aka, which column) has the deletion and the location of the exon (ref_qc is the IRanges object for exonic targets, use start(ref_qc) to get start positions and end(ref_qc) to get ending positions). Therefore you can plot the corresponding z-scores for that sample around that region to see if the signals are there.

BTW, did you check whether these exons get filtered out during your QC? You can look at the qcmat.txt file.

Also by saying loading IGV I meant loading CODEX’s calling results into IGV for visualization rather than the bam files themselves. See the bottom of https://sites.google.com/a/cornell.edu/yuchaojiang/home/research/codex  on how to do so but if you have a hard time (I feel you don’t use R as much) don’t worry about this — this is trivial and is only for sanity check by looking at the genome-wide results.

If after looking the z-scores you find that the signals are attenuated, then try optK=1 instead of 2. We know that a larger K tends to remove signals for common CNVs (in your case the CNV frequency is 14/97).

Cheers,
Yuchao

> Since the data is from humans in the study, I need to be sensitive about sharing the data. Our institution may consider de-identified WES data PHI (gray area) if it can be traced back to an individual from the fingerprint.

> Subject: RE: question on CODEX: tuning of optimal K?
>
> Dear Yuchao,
>

> Thanks for your prompt reply!

>
> 1.       Are your samples tumor samples or heterogeneous samples?
>

> No, my samples are from DNA on blood or fibroblast. I am interested in germline mutations. All samples are affected.

>
> 2.       How many exons does your heterozygous deletion span? Have you checked whether these exons get filtered out in the QC step? Have you looked at your normalization results? You can take the log ratio of Yhat[[optK]]/Y_qc and find the corresponding samples that you know harbor the deletions.
>

> One sample has a heterozygous deletion of exons 2-4, another with exons 15-20, another with homozygous intron7-exon15 (only deletion detected by CODEX), and multiple samples have heterozygous or homozygous deletion spanning entron17-intron18.
>
> How can I extract Yhat (very large list) and Y_qc (which row to choose?) for samples of interest?

>
> 3.       What range of K did you give CODEX to run? What is the optimal K decided by CODEX?
>

> K =  (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) with optk of 2.

>
> 4.       Have you loaded you calling results into IGV for visualization?
>

> Yes. The homozygous deletions are obvious. Heterozygous deletion shows sort of lower read depth compared to surrounding regions.
>
> Thanks
>
> Mari

>
>
>
> From: Jiang, Yuchao [mailto:yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu]
> Sent: Friday, February 26, 2016 5:09 PM
> To: Mari Mori
> Cc: codex_...@googlegroups.com
> Subject: RE: question on CODEX: tuning of optimal K?
>
> Hi Mari,
>
> Thanks for your interest in CODEX. As you can see from the in silico spike-in studies in the CODEX paper, CODEX has low sensitivity for common CNVs and we are currently working on a beta-version CODEX to solve this issue. Nevertheless, you GAA mutation is far from the common range of CNVs to be missed by CODEX. Can you give me some more background on your samples and the known heterozygous deletions?
>
> 1.       Are your samples tumor samples or heterogeneous samples? If so you need to use the ‘fraction’ mode and then filter you cnv calls based on the fractional copy number estimated. Do you have normal control? If yes, use normalize2 with index of normal samples instead of normalize.
> 2.       How many exons does your heterozygous deletion span? Have you checked whether these exons get filtered out in the QC step? Have you looked at your normalization results? You can take the log ratio of Yhat[[optK]]/Y_qc and find the corresponding samples that you know harbor the deletions.
> 3.       What range of K did you give CODEX to run? What is the optimal K decided by CODEX? You heterozygous deletions might be removed as a latent factor if you K is set too large/stringent.

> 4.       Have you loaded you calling results into IGV for visualization? See the bottom ofhttps://sites.google.com/a/cornell.edu/yuchaojiang/home/research/codex  on how to do so. For our CODEX paper, we didn’t use all 1092 samples from the 1000 Genomes Project but only selected <100 HapMap samples who also have SNP arrays as validations.

>
> Let me know if you have further questions. If you want to help you further and your data doesn’t involve human subjects / violates HIPPA, you can send me your save.image() r file and I might be able to help you figure out why.
>
> I am cc’ing our mailing list in case other people have similar questions.
>
> Cheers,
> Yuchao
>
> From: Mari Mori [mailto:mari...@duke.edu]
> Sent: Friday, February 26, 2016 2:49 PM
> To: Jiang, Yuchao <yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu>
> Subject: question on CODEX: tuning of optimal K?
>
> Dear Yuchao,
>
> I am using CODEX to demonstrate its sensitivity in detecting exonic deletions from WES data, and am writing to see if you have any advice on improving its sensitivity/specificity.
>
> I have 97 samples each with known compound heterozygous GAA mutations (molecularly confirmed patients with Pompe disease).
> 14 of them have exonic deletions in GAA (chromosome 17).
>
> I am trying to demonstrate if CODEX is able to detect these.
>
> The samples were sequenced in 2 batched and I ran CODEX for each batch of BAM files. For the first batch (36 samples), which contain 4 samples with exonic GAA deletions, CODEX did not detect any GAA deletion. It detected 679 del/dups in the entire chromosome 17. K max was 2.  For the second batch (61 samples), which contain 10 samples with  CODEX detected only one homozygous large deletion. It detected 1565 del/dups in the entire chromosome 17. I did not record K mas for this run.
>
> Do you think I should tweak the K max to improve the sensitivity and specificity?
>
> Also, in your publication, CODEX detected 91 del/dups in 1000 samples. This is strikingly low compared to my result in 97 samples. Did you adjust any parameter to get this result?
>
> Thanks for you help.
>
> Mari

>
>
>
>
>

> Medical Biochemical Genetics Fellow
> Division of Medical Genetics

messages.subject: Re: Question regarding CODEX error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew and Santhosh,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX! We’ve seen this error before and it is not due to algorithmic bug but rather the fact that the sample pool you adopt is too heterogenous. These samples are from different batches and most likely different sequencing centers too. As you can see from the first output, they have different read lengths. While CODEX is set to capture the artifact and biases in exome-sequencing data, it is recommended that different batches are processed separately. The reason that we see the error is essentially because the Poisson log-linear normalization model fails to converge during the iterative estimation procedure because your data is too noisy.

You can refer to here http://ftp.1000genomes.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/ftp/technical/working/20130606_sample_info/20130606_sample_info.xlsx for the batch and sequencing information from the 1000 Genomes Project. For CODEX to perform better, you can throw in more samples (again from the same center and ideally same batch), it can handle up to 300 at this stage. Also, use the phase 3 data, which have better quality.

Hope this clarifies. Let me know if you have further questions. I have cc’ing our mailing list so that other users who have similar questions will be able to see this.

Cheers,
Yuchao

messages.subject: RE: CODEX questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

It should your bed file input that leads to the error. The bed file should contain three columns (chr, start position, and end position), without header, and sorted by the start position. Each row corresponds to an exonic target.

It’s suggested that you run them in parallel and preferably on an HPC. You can of course loop through them but it may take longer.

Hope this clarifies! I am cc’ing our mailing list in case other users have similar questions.

Yuchao
